primary_cause: No clear Duke-specific headline Mar 15-17. Forced liquidation and liquidity panic overwhelming defensive utilities. Reuters described Mar 18 as cash is king session
secondary_factors: Recession fears implied weaker power demand growth. General de-risking out of rate-sensitive defensives
store_description: After exhaustive search no fresh Duke-specific catalyst in the March 15-17 window. DUK got caught in the broad cash-raising unwind on March 18 when even traditional defensive sectors sold off as investors dumped liquid names to raise cash.

primary_cause: Escalating realization COVID closures would hammer Disney parks and ESPN cash flow. Core businesses directly exposed — parks resorts theaters live sports and advertising
secondary_factors: General liquidity panic and recession fears. Reuters later noted parks swung from prior-year profit to expected multibillion-dollar loss
store_description: The drop looks mainly tied to investors repricing Disney unusually high exposure to physical attendance businesses and sports advertising as shutdowns spread. Market increasingly treating Disney less like a pure media and streaming story and more like a company with major parks resort box-office and ESPN disruption risk.

primary_cause: No fresh Deere-specific headline Mar 15-17. Cyclical industrial and recession exposure. Later withdrew 2020 guidance Mar 23
secondary_factors: Fears farm and construction equipment demand would weaken sharply. Dealers and customers would delay purchases
store_description: Deere nearly 10% decline fits the market violent repricing of economically sensitive industrials as COVID shutdowns intensified. No discrete Deere event in the prior 3 days so the best-supported read is investors discounting a fast deterioration in equipment demand.

primary_cause: Oil-price collapse driven by Saudi-Russia price war plus COVID demand destruction. Reuters called it dual supply-and-demand shock. Brent and WTI cratered
secondary_factors: Balance-sheet stress fears across whole energy complex. Indiscriminate selling
store_description: CVX 22.1% plunge was overwhelmingly about crude. By March 18 oil had already been smashed by the OPEC+ breakdown and pandemic-driven demand shock and investors were pricing a far weaker cash-flow outlook even for supermajors with better balance sheets.

primary_cause: Collapse in oil prices hitting upstream-heavy producer. Same energy shock as CVX. Pure upstream producer with more direct crude-price exposure than integrated majors
secondary_factors: Dividend and capex concerns. Broad energy credit stress
store_description: COP sold off because the market was rapidly repricing the earnings and cash-flow damage from sub-$30 crude conditions. Relative to integrated names Conoco had more direct exposure to the commodity shock which likely amplified the stock reaction.

primary_cause: No fresh Capital One-specific headline Mar 15-17. Expected spike in consumer credit losses during COVID recession. Market aggressively repricing consumer lenders
secondary_factors: Funding and liquidity fears. Zero-rate pressure on net interest margins
store_description: COF 17.8% drop looks mainly like a sector-level repricing of unsecured consumer credit risk not a discrete company headline. The market was assuming sharply higher delinquencies and charge-offs across credit cards and consumer finance as the economy shut down.

primary_cause: No fresh Emerson-specific headline Mar 15-17. Recession-driven selloff in industrial automation and capital spending names
secondary_factors: Energy exposure since Emerson also sells into oil and gas markets under extraordinary pressure. Continued March 16-18 collapse in economically sensitive industrial names
store_description: EMR likely fell because investors were simultaneously pricing a freeze in industrial capex and a major hit to energy-related end markets. No company-specific announcement in the prior 3 days strong enough to explain the move better than that combined macro and sector shock.

primary_cause: No negative Lilly-specific headline Mar 16-18. Pharma broadly seen as part of COVID treatment and vaccine race later. Broad de-risking and liquidation
secondary_factors: Profit-taking in defensives. Uncertainty around commercial pharma outlook during lockdowns
store_description: No strong Lilly-specific negative catalyst inside the March 16-18 window. The most defensible explanation is that LLY got dragged down in the final phase of the March liquidity panic when even relatively defensive healthcare names were being sold to raise cash.

primary_cause: No Lockheed-specific Mar 16-18 headline. Later Reuters confirmed COVID disrupted F-35 supply chain. Broad industrial and defense de-risking amid COVID uncertainty
secondary_factors: Early worries about supply-chain disruption and potential pressure on defense budgets
store_description: LMT decline appears more like a macro-driven defense and industrial selloff than a reaction to a new company announcement. Investors were beginning to discount possible production disruption and a tougher budget backdrop but the evidence for a precise stock-specific trigger is weak.

primary_cause: No fresh Altria-specific headline Mar 16-18. Modest move consistent with broad consumer-staples liquidation
secondary_factors: Existing skepticism around tobacco growth and regulatory overhangs but not a clear fresh headline
store_description: After searching no discrete March 16-18 Altria catalyst that cleanly explains a 3.2% drop. This looks more like MO being swept into a broad selloff in liquid large-cap defensives than a company-news-driven move.

primary_cause: No fresh Mar 16-18 Oracle-specific headline. Earnings were Mar 12 outside window. Broad tech selloff and liquidity stress
secondary_factors: Ongoing digestion of mixed earnings. Uncertainty about enterprise spending under COVID
store_description: ORCL 4.7% decline does not line up with a strong new March 16-18 catalyst. The most likely explanation is continued de-risking in large-cap tech plus lingering concern about enterprise software spending as companies braced for a sudden stop in the economy.

primary_cause: Reuters Mar 20 reported AT&T withdrew planned $4B share repurchase. Market likely already pricing same pressures on WarnerMedia and advertising and capital allocation
secondary_factors: General liquidity panic. Debt-heavy balance-sheet concerns. COVID pressure on AT&T media and advertising outlook
store_description: Even though the formal buyback withdrawal hit Reuters on March 20 T March 19 weakness fits investors moving ahead of that logic: preserve cash assume ad and media weakness and penalize leveraged balance sheets.

primary_cause: P&G already warned Feb about coronavirus hurting quarterly revenue and profit. No fresh Mar 16-18 headline. Broad market liquidation of defensives
secondary_factors: Existing supply-chain and overseas demand concerns
store_description: PG drop was probably not about a new headline in the prior three days so much as the market selling whatever was liquid including staples. The preexisting COVID supply-chain warning mattered to the narrative but the timing suggests March 19 was more forced selling.

primary_cause: No fresh UPS-specific Mar 16-18 headline. Macro slowdown fears affecting parcel and international logistics demand
secondary_factors: Cross-border disruption. Risk-off selling
store_description: UPS relatively modest 3% decline looks more like a recession and logistics-volume repricing than a reaction to a new company event. Investors were trying to handicap whether collapsing business activity would outweigh any temporary lift from home delivery.

primary_cause: No fresh KO-specific headline Mar 16-18. Reuters later made clear away-from-home channels highly exposed — restaurants theaters sports venues shutting down
secondary_factors: Broad defensive-stock liquidation. COVID closure risk to Coca-Cola away-from-home sales channels
store_description: KO drop was likely driven by the market realizing that a huge slice of soda consumption comes from venues being shut by lockdowns not just grocery shelves. That made Coca-Cola look less defensive than it usually does especially during the March cash crunch.

primary_cause: Pfizer and BioNTech announced vaccine collaboration Mar 17 but very early-stage. No negative Pfizer-specific headline. Broad-market liquidation
secondary_factors: General uncertainty around pharma supply chains and routine business disruption
store_description: PFE decline appears driven more by the marketwide scramble for cash than by any adverse company development in the prior three days. The vaccine partnership was too early to offset the fact that investors were selling even large defensive healthcare names.

primary_cause: No negative J&J-specific headline Mar 16-18. Broad-market and liquidity-driven selloff
secondary_factors: Temporary concern around medical-device and consumer-health demand disruption during lockdowns
store_description: Weak evidence for a company-specific bad-news trigger. The most likely explanation is that JNJ was sold alongside other mega-cap healthcare defensives during the late-March funding squeeze despite its strong balance sheet and eventual vaccine optionality.

primary_cause: U.S. tax filing deadline pushed from Apr 15 to Jul 15 announced Mar 20 — market may have been anticipating. Tax-season disruption from COVID and looming filing-delay decision
secondary_factors: Broad selloff in software and fintech-related names
store_description: INTU decline is one of the few March 19 moves where there is a plausible near-term business-specific angle: the COVID shock was disrupting the tax season and the federal filing date was about to be moved to July 15. Even though the formal announcement came the next day the market likely saw the extension coming.

primary_cause: No fresh Intel-specific Mar 16-18 headline. General semis and tech de-risking. Recession risk and uncertain supply-demand effects from COVID
secondary_factors: Uncertainty around supply chains and enterprise and PC demand mix
store_description: INTC move looks mostly macro rather than news-specific. The market was still trying to decide whether semis would benefit from stay-at-home computing demand or get hurt first by a global supply shock and then by a recession.

primary_cause: No fresh IBM-specific Mar 16-18 headline. Broad enterprise-tech de-risking amid COVID recession fears
secondary_factors: Concerns around slower consulting and services demand. Lingering skepticism about IBM growth profile
store_description: IBM 3.1% decline does not appear tied to a new company-specific event. The more likely driver was a marketwide repricing of enterprise IT spending and a general preference to sell slower-growth cyclical tech exposure during the late-March panic.
